title: Timely Persuasion with Opposing Senders: When Does Competition Help the Receiver?

paper.title: Timely Persuasion with Opposing Senders: When Does Competition Help the Receiver?
paper.abstract: Abstract Status updates let a receiver track a changing process, but a sender that controls when they are sent can steer the receiver’s estimate without misreporting. We study competition between two such senders with opposing preferences, who report on a binary continuous-time Markov chain using state-dependent Poisson rates under individual budgets. The receiver follows the reports through a zero-order-hold estimator only if this yields at least the long-run weighted correct-estimation utility of a prior-based default estimate. We model the interaction as a Stackelberg game in which the sender favored by this default leads, the opposing sender follows, and the receiver then selects its estimator. We characterize the pure-strategy equilibria in closed form. When the follower can obtain positive utility against a silent leader, limited state- 0 0 reporting by the leader merely frees part of the follower’s budget for state- 1 1 reports, so every optimal leader policy is either silence or full-budget state- 0 0 reporting, depending on explicit budget thresholds. A single sender with the same total budget leaves the receiver at its default utility, whereas the full-budget intervention outcome makes the receiver’s participation constraint slack and strictly improves its utility. At the intervention threshold, silence and full-budget intervention yield identical sender payoffs but different receiver utilities. Numerical results illustrate these regimes and compare equilibrium performance with a receiver-optimal reporting benchmark.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: When a receiver tracks a changing process through status updates, its estimate is only as current as the latest update. This has made the age of information a central performance measure [ 1 , 2 ] , and keeping information fresh is the natural goal when the sender wants the receiver to be accurate. A sender that instead has a stake in the receiver’s estimate can use timing to persuade without misreporting. In other words, by reporting favorable states promptly and unfavorable ones less frequently, it lets the receiver’s information go stale precisely when the state turns unfavorable. Since the receiver can ignore the updates altogether, the sender must still report unfavorable states often enough to keep the receiver following them [ 3 ] . A second sender with the opposite preference can supply these reports itself, but doing so also frees the first sender to report favorable states even more often. This raises two questions: when does the opposing sender choose to intervene, and when does its intervention improve the receiver’s estimation performance? We address these questions through a game in which two senders continuously observe a binary continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) and send truthful reports of its state to a common receiver as shown in Fig. 1 . Each sender’s strategy is a pair of state-dependent Poisson reporting rates, constrained by an individual budget on their sum. Irrespective of the source state, sender 1 is rewarded whenever the receiver’s estimate is 1 1 and sender 2 whenever it is 0 0 , so their payoffs are constant-sum. The receiver maximizes its long-run weighted correct-estimation utility by choosing between a zero-order-hold (ZOH) estimator, which retains the most recently reported state, and a default constant estimate chosen optimally under the stationary prior; throughout, we consider the regime in which this default estimate is 0 0 . The receiver therefore follows the reports only if ZOH estimation yields at least its default utility, a requirement we call the participation constraint (PC). Since this default already favors sender 2, we let it act as the leader and ask when it chooses to intervene. The resulting Stackelberg game has three stages: sender 2 commits to its reporting policy; sender 1, the follower, observes it and commits to its own; and the receiver observes both and selects its estimator. Both senders then report concurrently under these fixed policies. The receiver does not use information conveyed by the absence of reports, and our equilibrium and receiver-benefit results apply within this estimator architecture. Fig. 1 : System model with two competing senders and one receiver. Within the age-of-information literature, our model is closest to remote estimation, where sampling policies are designed to improve the receiver’s estimate of Wiener processes [ 4 ] , binary infection status [ 5 ] , and finite-state CTMCs under sampling rate constraints [ 6 ] . In our problem, the reporting rates are chosen by senders with opposing preferences over this estimate, so estimation performance is an equilibrium outcome rather than a design objective. As in Bayesian persuasion [ 7 ] and information design [ 8 ] , our senders commit to their policies in advance. Dynamic persuasion has been studied with partially informed receivers [ 9 ] , Markovian states [ 10 , 11 ] , and stochastic state revelations [ 12 ] . Ely [ 13 ] studies dynamic persuasion through messages about an evolving stochastic process, with a receiver that acts on its beliefs. Related formulations address sequential disclosure for change detection [ 14 ] , continuous-time persuasion through filtering [ 15 ] , and costly information provision without commitment to future actions [ 16 ] . In contrast to these models, which allow the sender to shape the receiver’s information through signal or disclosure design, our senders cannot alter the content of information and control only the timing of truthful state reports. Our prior work [ 3 ] studies this form of timely persuasion with a single sender, and we retain its source, reporting, and receiver models. There, whenever persuasion is feasible, the sender reports state 0 0 just often enough to make the PC bind, so the receiver gains nothing from following the reports. Asking whether competition can improve on this outcome connects our work to multi-sender persuasion, where the effect of competition on information revelation depends on the available signal structures [ 17 , 18 ] . Au and Kawai [ 19 ] show that increasing the number of symmetric senders leads to more aggressive disclosure in their model, and Li and Norman [ 20 ] characterize equilibrium outcomes under sequential persuasion. In the control literature, Velicheti et al. [ 21 ] study simultaneous sender commitments with Gaussian information and quadratic objectives, including a dynamic extension, and establish a receiver benefit from competition relative to cooperation among the senders. Our senders instead commit sequentially to the rates of truthful reports. Since J 1 + J 2 = 1 J_{1}+J_{2}=1 , maximizing the sum of sender payoffs does not select a reporting policy. We therefore compare the receiver’s equilibrium utility with that under a single sender with the same total budget. We answer both questions posed at the outset. For the first, we derive the follower’s best response and characterize the pure-strategy Stackelberg equilibria in closed form. When the follower can obtain positive utility on its own, the leader’s state- 0 0 reports first help the follower by freeing its budget for state- 1 1 reports and hurt it only once they alone exceed what participation requires. The leader therefore chooses between silence and full-budget state- 0 0 reporting. We identify a threshold on the follower’s budget below which silence is optimal regardless of the leader’s budget, and a second threshold governing intervention above it. For the second, whenever the full-budget intervention outcome is optimal, the leader’s state- 0 0 reports make the PC slack and strictly increase the receiver’s utility. In contrast, the optimal single-sender benchmark leaves the receiver at its default utility. At the intervention threshold, the two optimal leader policies yield identical sender payoffs but different receiver utilities. Numerical results illustrate these regimes and show that an appropriate budget division can attain the receiver-optimal reporting benchmark for the parameters considered.

sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: We studied competition between two senders that influence a receiver through the timing of truthful reports about a binary continuous-time Markov source. We characterized the Stackelberg equilibria in closed form. When the follower can obtain positive utility against a silent leader, the leader’s state- 0 0 reports initially help the follower by reducing the reporting effort needed for participation, so every optimal leader policy is either silence or full-budget state- 0 0 reporting, with explicit budget thresholds determining which. In the low-budget regime, equilibrium leader policies can be nonunique, but all such equilibria leave the receiver at its default utility. When the full-budget intervention outcome is optimal, it makes the participation constraint slack and strictly improves the receiver’s utility relative to a single sender with the same total budget. In our numerical example, an appropriate budget division attains a receiver-optimal reporting benchmark. Future work will consider opposing senders that allocate their budgets across multiple heterogeneous sources, alternative commitment orders, and receivers that also exploit information conveyed by the absence of reports.

Abstract Status updates let a receiver track a changing process, but a sender that controls when they are sent can steer the receiver’s estimate without misreporting. We study competition between two such senders with opposing preferences, who report on a binary continuous-time Markov chain using state-dependent Poisson rates under individual budgets. The receiver follows the reports through a zero-order-hold estimator only if this yields at least the long-run weighted correct-estimation utility of a prior-based default estimate. We model the interaction as a Stackelberg game in which the sender favored by this default leads, the opposing sender follows, and the receiver then selects its estimator. We characterize the pure-strategy equilibria in closed form. When the follower can obtain positive utility against a silent leader, limited state- 0 0 reporting by the leader merely frees part of the follower’s budget for state- 1 1 reports, so every optimal leader policy is either silence or full-budget state- 0 0 reporting, depending on explicit budget thresholds. A single sender with the same total budget leaves the receiver at its default utility, whereas the full-budget intervention outcome makes the receiver’s participation constraint slack and strictly improves its utility. At the intervention threshold, silence and full-budget intervention yield identical sender payoffs but different receiver utilities. Numerical results illustrate these regimes and compare equilibrium performance with a receiver-optimal reporting benchmark. I Introduction When a receiver tracks a changing process through status updates, its estimate is only as current as the latest update. This has made the age of information a central performance measure [ 1 , 2 ] , and keeping information fresh is the natural goal when the sender wants the receiver to be accurate. A sender that instead has a stake in the receiver’s estimate can use timing to persuade without misreporting. In other words, by reporting favorable states promptly and unfavorable ones less frequently, it lets the receiver’s information go stale precisely when the state turns unfavorable. Since the receiver can ignore the updates altogether, the sender must still report unfavorable states often enough to keep the receiver following them [ 3 ] . A second sender with the opposite preference can supply these reports itself, but doing so also frees the first sender to report favorable states even more often. This raises two questions: when does the opposing sender choose to intervene, and when does its intervention improve the receiver’s estimation performance? We address these questions through a game in which two senders continuously observe a binary continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) and send truthful reports of its state to a common receiver as shown in Fig. 1 . Each sender’s strategy is a pair of state-dependent Poisson reporting rates, constrained by an individual budget on their sum. Irrespective of the source state, sender 1 is rewarded whenever the receiver’s estimate is 1 1 and sender 2 whenever it is 0 0 , so their payoffs are constant-sum. The receiver maximizes its long-run weighted correct-estimation utility by choosing between a zero-order-hold (ZOH) estimator, which retains the most recently reported state, and a default constant estimate chosen optimally under the stationary prior; throughout, we consider the regime in which this default estimate is 0 0 . The receiver therefore follows the reports only if ZOH estimation yields at least its default utility, a requirement we call the participation constraint (PC). Since this default already favors sender 2, we let it act as the leader and ask when it chooses to intervene. The resulting Stackelberg game has three stages: sender 2 commits to its reporting policy; sender 1, the follower, observes it and commits to its own; and the receiver observes both and selects its estimator. Both senders then report concurrently under these fixed policies. The receiver does not use information conveyed by the absence of reports, and our equilibrium and receiver-benefit results apply within this estimator architecture. Fig. 1 : System model with two competing senders and one receiver. Within the age-of-information literature, our model is closest to remote estimation, where sampling policies are designed to improve the receiver’s estimate of Wiener processes [ 4 ] , binary infection status [ 5 ] , and finite-state CTMCs under sampling rate constraints [ 6 ] . In our problem, the reporting rates are chosen by senders with opposing preferences over this estimate, so estimation performance is an equilibrium outcome rather than a design objective. As in Bayesian persuasion [ 7 ] and information design [ 8 ] , our senders commit to their policies in advance. Dynamic persuasion has been studied with partially informed receivers [ 9 ] , Markovian states [ 10 , 11 ] , and stochastic state revelations [ 12 ] . Ely [ 13 ] studies dynamic persuasion through messages about an evolving stochastic process, with a receiver that acts on its beliefs. Related formulations address sequential disclosure for change detection [ 14 ] , continuous-time persuasion through filtering [ 15 ] , and costly information provision without commitment to future actions [ 16 ] . In contrast to these models, which allow the sender to shape the receiver’s information through signal or disclosure design, our senders cannot alter the content of information and control only the timing of truthful state reports. Our prior work [ 3 ] studies this form of timely persuasion with a single sender, and we retain its source, reporting, and receiver models. There, whenever persuasion is feasible, the sender reports state 0 0 just often enough to make the PC bind, so the receiver gains nothing from following the reports. Asking whether competition can improve on this outcome connects our work to multi-sender persuasion, where the effect of competition on information revelation depends on the available signal structures [ 17 , 18 ] . Au and Kawai [ 19 ] show that increasing the number of symmetric senders leads to more aggressive disclosure in their model, and Li and Norman [ 20 ] characterize equilibrium outcomes under sequential persuasion. In the control literature, Velicheti et al. [ 21 ] study simultaneous sender commitments with Gaussian information and quadratic objectives, including a dynamic extension, and establish a receiver benefit from competition relative to cooperation among the senders. Our senders instead commit sequentially to the rates of truthful reports. Since J 1 + J 2 = 1 J_{1}+J_{2}=1 , maximizing the sum of sender payoffs does not select a reporting policy. We therefore compare the receiver’s equilibrium utility with that under a single sender with the same total budget. We answer both questions posed at the outset. For the first, we derive the follower’s best response and characterize the pure-strategy Stackelberg equilibria in closed form. When the follower can obtain positive utility on its own, the leader’s state- 0 0 reports first help the follower by freeing its budget for state- 1 1 reports and hurt it only once they alone exceed what participation requires. The leader therefore chooses between silence and full-budget state- 0 0 reporting. We identify a threshold on the follower’s budget below which silence is optimal regardless of the leader’s budget, and a second threshold governing intervention above it. For the second, whenever the full-budget intervention outcome is optimal, the leader’s state- 0 0 reports make the PC slack and strictly increase the receiver’s utility. In contrast, the optimal single-sender benchmark leaves the receiver at its default utility. At the intervention threshold, the two optimal leader policies yield identical sender payoffs but different receiver utilities. Numerical results illustrate these regimes and show that an appropriate budget division can attain the receiver-optimal reporting benchmark for the parameters considered.
